newsitem.title: USA: Congressman considers impeachment of Clinton, Gore.
newsitem.headline: Congressman considers impeachment of Clinton, Gore.

text.p: A Republican Congressman from Georgia said on Friday he had asked the House Judiciary Committee to begin preliminary steps for consideration of the impeachment of President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore.

Representative Bob Barr said he had written to Judiciary Committee Chairman Henry Hyde, R-Illinois, asking for a committee meeting to discuss whether campaign fundraising activities by Clinton and Gore warranted impeachment proceedings.

"It is important to keep in mind that my request is a very measured and judicious one clearly warranted by the evidence available," Barr said. "I am not demanding that impeachment proceedings begin at this time. The time has come, however, to take this important preliminary step."

"There is no question in my mind that the alarming pattern of abuse of the political process by this White House is unprecedented," Barr said. He was referring to reports of alleged improper fundraising activities at the White House and calls by Gore from the White House to solicit funds.
The committee said Hyde was reviewing Barr's letter.
Under the impeachment process, the House Judiciary Committee would have to conduct an investigation and then vote on whether to impeach Clinton and Gore.

If the committee approved one or more articles of impeachment and the full House adopted them, a trial would be held on the charges with members of the Senate as the jury. A two-thirds majority of the 100 senators is needed to remove an impeached official.

The last time the impeachment process was used against a president was in 1974 when the Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment against Richard Nixon. He resigned before the full House could vote on them.
Barr, a former intelligence analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency and U.S. attorney in Georgia, is serving his second term in Congress.

Other committees in both the House and Senate and the Justice Department are investigating the fundraising activities. Attorney General Janet Reno has been asked by several members of Congress from both parties to request appointment of independent counsel, but she has said there was not enough evidence of illegal activity to take such a step.
